events.headline: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
events.evidence: The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. This was the second time the province of Alberta had challenged the act, which sets out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. "While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the [Impact Assessment Act] creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects," the court wrote. Canada's top court rules environmental impact law unconstitutional "This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction." The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren't constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. "The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project," the court wrote. Alberta challenge to federal project review law being heard in court, again Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta in its legal challenge. events.headline: Ontario will officially begin removing Toronto bike lanes on Tuesday | CBC News
events.evidence: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes. Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says. A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct. "Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said. T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. "That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said. The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.' Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke. "Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes." events.headline: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
events.evidence: A protester shout slogans as they are detained and taken in a police vehicle during a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption NEW DELHI — Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities. Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start. The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Vipin/AP hide caption Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained. "We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world's largest democracy. events.headline: New Liberal major projects bill clears first vote, heads to special committee | CBC News
events.evidence: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee. The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country. The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year. The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets. Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill. Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation. events.headline: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
events.evidence: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. events.headline: BRICS: Cabinet’s decision is that we should begin as a partner country - Ablakwa
events.evidence: We want to start as a partner country, and then we will gradually progress into full membership as the situation evolves The Minister of Foreign Affairs Samuel Okudzeto Abklakwa has explained that Ghana will join BRICS as a partner country. According to him, Cabinet's decision forms part of the government’s efforts to expand Ghana’s economic options and diversify its international partnerships. He said the move would also strengthen Ghana’s engagement with countries in the Global South and create opportunities for deeper South-South cooperation. "We want to start as a partner country, and then we will gradually progress into full membership as the situation evolves," he said on the Key Points on TV3 Saturday October 10. “The major highlight, which I am disclosing to the Ghanaian people for the first time, is that the Cabinet of President John Dramani Mahama has decided that Ghana will be joining BRICS,” he said. Ablakwa explained that Ghana believes membership of the bloc, which brings together major emerging economies, could provide the country with alternative economic and diplomatic partnerships. “We believe that joining India in BRICS will give us economic options, will diversify our base and our partnerships, and will also allow us to have more cooperation within the Global South framework, as far as South-South engagements are concerned,” he added. events.headline: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
events.evidence: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult. events.headline: City Council approves Toronto's 2026 budget with $63.1-billion capital plan, frozen TTC fares
events.evidence: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also proposes what she called a fairer approach to funding city services, asking "empty home speculators and luxury property buyers" — the top 2 per cent of all buyers — to contribute more. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. events.headline: US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
events.evidence: US military jet strikes stern of commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman ‘without harming the crew’, CENTCOM says. United States forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew “ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran”, according to Central Command (CENTCOM). A US military fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday, “fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew”, CENTCOM said in a statement. The vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after “having previously departed an Iranian port”. CENTCOM said its forces resumed their blockade against all ships “entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14”, disabling four commercial vessels and turning around 135 ships during “three months of strict enforcement”. US forces also destroyed 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) “multibillion-dollar shadow network” over the same period, CENTCOM said. US Senator Chris Murphy questioned the military strike, writing on X: “What is this all for? Why are taxpayers paying billions to hit commercial ships?” The agency did not specify the origin of the ship or the number of people killed or injured, adding that authorities were investigating the incident amid a recent rise in attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz. Ships in the Gulf attempting to cross the strait, which is the sole maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region, have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel began the war in late February. The Strait of Hormuz remains vital to the global economy, with about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the passage before the war began.

events.headline: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports and lower tariffs for some European exports to China | Fortune
events.evidence: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said. Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains. The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.” The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year. China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. events.headline: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
events.evidence: UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures. But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.

events.headline: Bangladesh hands UAE's DP World key port contract after years of delay
events.evidence: Deal aims to modernize facility, but foreign stake in strategic asset has faced pushback A deal between Bangladesh and DP World for the Dubai-based logistics company to operate and maintain the New Mooring Container Terminal at the country's largest port comes after years of delays, labor protests and a legal challenge that had left the concession at Chattogram Port in limbo. (Nikkei montage/Source photos by Getty Images) DHAKA -- Bangladesh signed a 15-year deal with DP World on Thursday for the Dubai-based logistics company to operate and maintain the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at the country's largest port, ending years of negotiations over one of the country's most politically sensitive infrastructure projects.

events.headline: Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
events.evidence: RIYADH, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said. Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said. The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis - an assertion denied by the Syrian president's media adviser, Ahmad Zaidan, in a post on X following the publication of this story. In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war. "Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement. The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment. Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom. events.headline: BAERA clears first criticality for Rooppur Unit-1
events.evidence: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Bangladesh has cleared a major hurdle in commissioning its first nuclear power plant, with the country’s nuclear regulator granting approval for the ‘first criticality’ process for Unit 1 of the 2,400 MW Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP). “We have issued the approval named – B2 – for Unit-1 to move forward in the second stage of rigorous scrutiny before initiation of its commercial operation,” BAERA Chairman Mahmudul Hasan told The Financial Express on Thursday. The Unit-1 will have to attain two more certifications, namely C and D, before initiating commercial operation, said the BAERA chief without elaborating. The B2 certification marks a significant step toward bringing the country’s maiden nuclear power facility into operation. First criticality is the stage at which a reactor achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction for the first time, a prerequisite for commercial power generation. Project officials said the approval had been delayed due to technical complications involving the reactor’s pilot-operated relief and safety valves, a critical component of the plant’s safety systems. Russian experts were brought in to resolve the issue, and the system subsequently passed a series of tests, clearing the way for regulatory authorisation. According to project sources, first criticality has long been regarded as one of the most challenging milestones for the Rooppur project. As part of the physical start-up process, the reactor will initially be operated at less than one percent of its designed thermal capacity. Engineers and regulators will closely monitor and verify key reactor parameters, safety systems, control equipment and operational performance during the first criticality stage. Electricity generation would initially begin at around three percent capacity before being gradually raised to between 20 and 30 percent, at which point power can be supplied to the national grid. Once Rooppur starts supplying power to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world’s 33rd nuclear power-producing nation, opening a new chapter in the country’s energy security and technological advancement. The long-awaited achievement is also expected to strengthen Bangladesh’s efforts to diversify its energy mix and ensure a more stable long-term electricity supply.

events.headline: Canada Gazette, Part 1, Volume 160, Number 41: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
events.evidence: On July 2, 2026, the Government of Alberta submitted a proposal to the Major Projects Office (MPO), asking Canada to consider the proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline (the Project) for listing as a national interest project under the Building Canada Act (the Act, or the BCA). This proposal followed a November 27, 2025 Memorandum of Understanding and a May 15, 2026 Implementation Agreement completed between Canada and Alberta, in which both Canada and Alberta affirmed the importance of augmenting Canada’s export of domestic oil to foreign markets as one element in a national strategy to meet a pivotal global moment. The Project is a proposed interprovincial pipeline capable of transporting approximately 1 million barrels per day (MMb/d) of Canadian crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia (BC), where the oil would be transferred to vessels and shipped to global markets. The Governor in Council (GIC), pursuant to subsection 5(1) of the Act and on the recommendation of the Minister responsible under the Act, the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada — the Honourable Dominic LeBlanc (the Minister) — amends Schedule 1 of the Act to add the Project as a national interest project, as specified in the Order in Council to which this Explanatory Note is appended. The objective of this Order is to enable the Project’s timely development by bringing it within the regulatory framework of the Act, based on the GIC’s determination that the Project is in Canada’s national interest and that the Act thus supplies an appropriate framework to structure applicable federal regulatory authorizations, ensure appropriate environmental safeguards, and meet Canada’s constitutional obligations to Indigenous peoples. The Act was enacted by Parliament on June 26, 2025, to provide a simplified, direct, timely and comprehensive process to secure federal regulatory authorization for projects determined to be of vital interest to Canada. The legislation provides Canada with a means to confront the reality that nation-building natural resource and infrastructure projects have long faced complicated, cumbersome and time-consuming federal regulatory processes. While this problem was already acute, it became pressing following the rupture of prior stable forms of international economic integration and trade brought about by the sudden change in policy orientation of the United States (US), Canada’s largest trading partner and the market for the majority of Canadian exports. This reorientation of federal decision-making occurs within the framework of Canada’s respect for Aboriginal and treaty rights as recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 ; its duty to consult with Indigenous peoples; its commitment to reconciliation; and its respect for the rights set out in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. These decisions can be taken only after Canada has met its duty to consult and, where appropriate, accommodate Indigenous peoples whose Aboriginal and treaty rights may be adversely affected by the carrying out of the projects to which the decisions relate. First, the GIC’s decision to list a national interest project under Schedule 1 of the Act (a listing decision) results in immediate, deemed fulfillment of substantive prerequisites to the release of federal permits and authorizations listed in Schedule 2 of the Act. The Project is a proposed interprovincial pipeline to transport approximately 1 million barrels per day (MMb/d) of crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia. Two marine berths will be designed to support Very Large Crude Carriers; these vessels typically have a capacity of two million barrels. Trans Mountain Corporation (TMC), Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission (APMC), and Pembina Pipeline Corporation (Pembina) [together, the Ownership Group] will form and lead a new jointly owned company: In addition, a minimum of 10 percent ownership interest in the Project will be offered for purchase to Indigenous peoples.
